title: Should You Rebrand or Explain What Your Company Already Does?
seoTitle: When Should You Rebrand? What Kia’s Case Can Teach You | CRUDA
description: What changed at Kia, how much revenue grew, and how to tell when your business needs a rebrand or a clearer explanation.
html:
Should You Rebrand or Explain What Your Company Already Does?

Kia changed its identity while expanding its offering. Their case helps you decide what to change when buyers continue to see your company as before.

You find out about a tender when it is already closed. You know the buyer, your team could deliver the project and you have a similar case to prove it. When you ask why they didn't call you, the answer is almost a compliment. When they need parts, they always think of you. When they need someone to install and maintain the whole system, they make a different list.

It's an easy situation to recognize if your company grew by selling to the same customers. Inside, the team has been adding capabilities for years. On the outside, the first version of the business is still the easiest to remember. And a portion of the billing you want to earn is decided before sales even submits a proposal.

When is it appropriate to do a rebranding?

How do you know if you need a rebranding? First show what the company can already do. If a clear test changes what you would be hired for, start by better explaining the offer. If the previous perception persists and is reinforced by the name, identity or presentation of your services, it is worth reviewing the brand. If you still lack the ability to deliver on the promise, resolve that part of the business first.

In this article

  1. What changed at Kia
  2. Why so many read “KN”
  3. How much did your turnover grow?
  4. How to diagnose your company
  5. How we resolved a brand decision at Mannheim Trading
  6. What to decide before approving the budget
  7. Frequently asked questions
  8. Sources and scope

What changed at Kia before changing the logo?

Kia is a South Korean automaker. In 2020, it announced Plan S, a strategy that gave more weight to electric vehicles and contemplated new mobility services. In January 2021 it presented its new identity and shortened the name from Kia Motors to Kia. That same year the EV6 arrived, an electric car developed on a platform designed for this type of vehicle. The buyer had something concrete to look at, compare and try. Kia Announcement 2021 · History of Plan S and the EV6.

When Kia dropped Motors from its name, it had already announced what it wanted to build and how it was going to expand its offering. Identity gave a visible form to that change. The EV6 allowed the buyer to evaluate it on their own.

The change also reached the place where you buy a car. In France, Kia documented how the identity was transferred to the dealerships, with changes in the exhibition and service spaces. There appears a question that is useful to any CEO. If your brand changes tomorrow, at what point during the purchase will the customer notice that the company has also changed? Kia Francia, deployment in dealerships.

In a company, positioning is the space you want to occupy in the minds of your customers and, if you aspire to a deeper connection, also in their hearts. Identity brings together the signals with which you are recognized, such as your name and design. A rebranding reviews in a coordinated manner how that brand is presented. It can accompany a repositioning, as in Kia. It can also solve a narrower problem, such as an identity that makes it difficult to recognize a valid offer.

Why did so many people read "KN" in Kia's new logo?

Imagine that you have a car ahead of you at a traffic light. In the trunk you see two black shapes joined together. The last letter looks like an N. When you get home, you search KN car to find out what brand the car was. That search ended up being part of the history of rebranding.

Kia had replaced the oval and separate letters with a continuous stroke, similar to a signature. I wanted the design to express movement. On the street, some people read something else. At the end of 2022, searches for KN car became news and the discussion about the logo jumped from networks to specialized media. Kia confirmed to MotorTrend that it detected a spike in searches around the coverage and that negative mentions later returned to previous levels. Original Kia announcement · Kia statements to MotorTrend.

Was it intentional? Kia explained that it was looking for a more distinctive signature and that it considered the result legible. Their public statements leave the reading "KN" as a consequence of the design. CRUDA's reading is that the controversy gave additional exposure to the change: there were people who saw the emblem, wanted to find out who was behind it, and came to Kia. The confusion came at a real cost in readability, and that same curiosity gave it a second wave of attention.

What followed matters more than the peak. The brand maintained that signature while the EV6 gave way to the EV9 and the EV3. In its 2026 investor presentation, Kia reported that more people remembered the brand without being shown a list of names than in 2021. It's a sign that Kia gained presence in buyers' memories during the relaunch. Presentation measures brand recall, so a different question remains open: how many people today recognize the isolated emblem. Kia CEO Investor Day 2026, evolution of spontaneous memory.

If you run an industrial company, the question appears in a smaller form. A buyer can comment on your new identity and still not know that you now install the entire system. Try the brand on a card, a proposal or the front of a team. Ask her what company she thinks she is looking at, what she understands she does, and what project she would call her for. There you can see if the attention is helping to open the commercial conversation you were looking for.

How much did Kia’s revenue grow?

Kia's consolidated revenue increased from 59.2 trillion won in 2020 to 114.1 trillion won in 2025. The increase was around 93% in nominal currency. Between 2024 and 2025, turnover rose by 6.2%, while operating profit fell by 28.3%. Revenue growth and profitability tell different parts of the story. Kia, figures for 2020 and 2021 · Kia, consolidated statements from 2022 to 2025.

These figures do not allow the growth to be attributed to the logo. They measure all of Kia. In its presentation to investors, the company reported that between 2021 and 2025, wholesale volume rose from 2.78 to 3.14 million vehicles, while its average sales price rose from 27.1 to 38.4 million won. Kia links the average price to factors such as product quality and a greater share of SUVs and electrified vehicles. That reading is from the company. Kia, presentation to investors.

The commercial balance for the period was positive in income and volume. The rebranding gave a visible identity to the transformation, and the conversation around “KN” amplified its exposure. To estimate how much each thing contributed to sales, changes in perception and purchase consideration would have to be contrasted with what happened with products, prices, volume and distribution. The case is useful because it shows an identity accompanied by business decisions that buyers could verify.

How do you distinguish a brand problem from a communication problem?

In CRUDA, this part of the diagnosis comes from the 5 Cs. For this decision, we start with what the company can already do, what the category takes for granted, and what the customer understood. We review a missed opportunity or a tender to which the company was not even invited. The conversation with sales helps to locate the exact moment in which it was left out.

Choose the type of client or project you want to win. Show buyers of that profile how the company presents itself today. Ask them to tell you what job they would call you for, what they wouldn't call you for, and what they would need to see to change their mind. Then show concrete proof of your ability and ask again.

Three possible responses from a buyer

Imagine an industrial company that previously provided components and now also installs and maintains the complete system. Three buyers may react differently to the same project.

What you hearWhat would I do first?
"I didn't know they could take care of everything." After seeing the case, I would include you in the next tender.Better explain the offer. Incorporate the test into the website, the proposals and the sales story.
"I understand what they do, but I always look at them as a parts supplier." The reading is repeated and the way of presenting the lines reinforces it.Try a repositioning. Evaluate what brand signals support that association and what should be changed.
«I understand the offer. What I don't see is who responds if something goes wrong.Resolve and demonstrate that capacity. If that responsibility already exists, demonstrate who is responsible and under what conditions. If no one can take it on, resolve that part of the operation first.

These answers can coexist. A company may need a better business proposition today and a new identity later. The criterion for ordering work is to identify what leaves it out of the opportunities that it can attend to.

When should a new venture have its own brand? The case of Mannheim Trading

José Mannheim knew the problem from the inside. He had co-founded the company that gave rise to AGP and knew what materials safety glass manufacturers needed. His new business was going to supply them. The question it brought to us was how to bring the credibility it already had in the industry to a company with its own commercial proposition.

In CRUDA we saw two decisions. The last name could explain who was behind it. The website had to show why a manufacturer would call the new company. This required making visible what inputs it offered, what applications they were used for and how to request a quote. That's where the name Mannheim Trading, the value proposition, the identity and the website came from. Mannheim Trading Case.

Kia wanted to expand on what the market associated with a household name. Mannheim Trading needed the buyer to understand a new company without losing sight of its founder's experience. In both cases, the decision begins when you can say what the buyer needs to understand and what they will find to verify it.

What do you decide before approving the budget?

Go back to the client who recommends you for small jobs. Show them the most demanding project your team has already delivered and explain what responsibility the company took on from start to finish.

If after seeing it I would recommend you for a larger job, have that test come sooner, when the buyer is still putting together their list of suppliers. If the old image continues to weigh heavily even in the face of evidence, investigate what signs keep it alive.

There you will have an assignment that explains what perception you need to change, in whom and for what business decision. With this assignment you can discuss whether the work begins with the commercial proposal, positioning or identity.

Frequently asked questions about rebranding and positioning

Are rebranding and repositioning the same thing?

A repositioning seeks to change the place you occupy in the customer's mind. A rebranding changes how the brand is presented, for example its name, its identity or its way of expressing itself. They can be part of the same project if the current signals support the perception you want to change.

Can I improve my positioning with the same logo?

Yes. If compelling proof changes what you'd be hired for, you can start by making it visible on the website, in proposals, and in sales conversations.

Did the logo increase Kia's sales?

The controversy amplified the exhibition of the emblem. Public accounts show how much Kia's turnover grew during the change. To attribute a part to the logo, evidence would be needed to separate its effect from changes in product, price, volume and distribution.

Sources and scope

  • The timeline is based on the official Plan S and EV6 announcements, 2021 identity and Kia press material credited in the images.
  • The figures are nominal consolidated income for complete years. Kia's 2023 report covers the base of 2020 and 2021. The consolidated financial summary covers 2022 to 2025. Average volume and price are from the investor presentation and are for 2021–2025.
  • The discussion about “KN” is documented with Kia's response to MotorTrend. The spontaneous memory corresponds to the brand monitoring presented by Kia at its Investor Day 2026.
  • The bidding example is hypothetical. CRUDA's work for Mannheim Trading is documented in the case study and on the company website.

title: Clients Still Ask for Me. How Do I Introduce Them to the Team?
seoTitle: How to Reduce Founder Dependence in Key Client Relationships | CRUDA
description: A lighting case and a practical way to give your senior team visible authority while keeping the trust of key clients.
html:
Clients Still Ask for Me. How Do I Introduce Them to the Team?

Your name opens the door. How to give the team authority with key clients while still being present where it matters most.

Imagine the scene. You introduce the client to the senior person who will lead their project. The client greets them, looks at the drawings, and turns to you as soon as the first difficult question comes up.

You know who did the work, who saw the problem first and who has the best judgment to solve it. The client has been seeing something else for years. Every time a delicate decision had to be made, you were there. Now he wants to know if that part of the deal still stands.

How to reduce dependence on the founder without losing customer trust?

Introduce the senior person while you are still involved in the relationship. Give them the authority to explain and resolve a real decision in front of the client. Clarify what they can decide, what remains under your supervision and when you intervene again. The client needs to see how that agreement works on their own project.

In this article

  • What does the client fear losing?
  • What to do at the next meeting
  • How to show the team's judgment before selling
  • What changes when the face of the company is a director
  • Frequently asked questions
  • Sources and scope

What does the client fear losing?

At one lighting company we worked with, the founder was the point of contact that many clients in a new market were looking for. There was already a senior account executive. Still, in the most demanding projects, the client wanted to meet the founder from the beginning. There his presence had a commercial function. It helped open up relationships that the team was still building.

In its home market, the situation was different. Clients knew and trusted several people on the team. But when the founder began to dedicate more time to expansion, some major project clients wanted to know if she would continue to oversee theirs. The request made sense. In lighting, a late decision can affect what is already planned on site. The client wanted to know who was going to respond when that happened.

In CRUDA's proposal, the founder retained creative direction and supervision in decisive projects. The senior team gained visibility for their work and the criteria with which they solved problems. For each account, the question was which decision the customer needed to continue to see in the hands of the founder and which one they could start entrusting to someone else.

There is evidence that it matters who is directly involved in a business relationship. Joseph Raffiee studied public affairs firms in the United States and found that clients with direct ties to more people in the firm were less likely to follow a professional when he changed firms. The study analyzes employee departures in a specific sector. For a director, leave a specific question. How many people in your company have resolved something directly with that client? Research by Joseph Raffiee

What to do at the next meeting

I went back to the plans. Imagine that the architect wants to change the light in a room when the ceiling is already closed. You give the floor to the senior designer. She shows where you can intervene, what effect each option would have and which one you would choose. The decision is within your reach and you can close it with the client at that time. If a modification appears that changes the budget or requires creative revision, the client already knows whose turn it is to decide.

Try this journey on an account where the customer already knows you. Choose a decision that is important to him and that the team can resolve. If the decision is minor, you barely see that someone carried out a procedure. If the team needs to ask your permission live, confirm that you are still the only one able to close the topic.

How to show the team's judgment before selling

In the case of lighting, we proposed disassembling real projects on LinkedIn and Instagram. The post would start with the problem the team needed to solve, show the options, and be signed by the senior designer who made the decision. Thus, an architect who still only knew the founder could see how the person who was going to work with him thought.

To bring it to your company, I chose a case where the team made a decision that a difficult client would understand and value. Show the plan, evidence or detail that can be shared. Explain what was at stake and who held the judgment. Use the piece when presenting to the team in a proposal or before the first meeting. The next time that client sees the senior person's name, they will have a reason to listen to it.

What changes when the face of the company is a director

The problem also appears when the person who opens the door is a country director. A company can have years of experience and specialized teams, and the client continues to call someone they know to find out if someone is going to take charge.

Ask what they need from that person. If you want to confirm a specification, introduce it to the person who can decide it. If you need someone to authorize a change in conditions, explain who has that authority. The first call shows you where in the business that relationship is still focused. How to get customers to ask for your B2B brand

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to stop participating in large projects?

Define in which decisions your presence adds value to the client. You can maintain creative, commercial or technical supervision on important projects and give the team a clear scope to decide and respond to the rest.

How can I tell if the handoff is working?

See who the next important query is directed to. If the client goes directly to the senior person and that person can resolve it within what was agreed upon, you already have an observable signal in that account.

Before your next meeting

I chose an account. Ask the client when they expect you to be present. With your team, choose a decision where the senior person already has discretion and authority. When the difficult question comes, stay in the room and let her answer it. Then watch where the client's head turns when they do the next one.

Sources and scope

  • The lighting case comes from the work of CRUDA. Names, markets and identifiable projects are omitted. The editorial actions are described as part of the proposal. The ceiling scene is hypothetical.
  • Joseph Raffiee studied relationships between public affairs firms, professionals and clients in the United States. The article uses that evidence as context about shared relationships. Original study

title: How Do You Stand Out in B2B When Everyone Promises Quality and Service?
seoTitle: How to Differentiate Your B2B Company and Prove Its Value | CRUDA
description: Use the AGP sGlass example and a practical framework to turn promises about quality and service into evidence buyers can compare.
html:
How Do You Stand Out in B2B When Everyone Promises Quality and Service?

A value proposition gives the buyer something they can check before choosing. An example of AGP sGlass and a test for your next quote.

The quote comes back with one line underlined. It’s the price. You've been manufacturing for twenty years, your team knows how to solve problems that other suppliers send back to the customer, and you've already delivered orders that are much more complicated than this one. But the person comparing the proposals has three documents in front of him. In all three it says "quality and service."

Ask sales to reconstruct where that difference was on paper. Maybe someone explained it at the meeting. If the person preparing the recommendation cannot find or verify it, the figure on the last page ends up being the easiest to defend.

How to demonstrate the value proposition of a B2B company?

Choose a risk that the buyer must resolve to approve the purchase. Show what your company does to reduce it, how it can be verified and under what conditions it is met. Put that proof next to the offer so that the buyer can use it even when you are not in the room.

In this article

  • What quality means when you buy armored glass
  • What proof does each person need to decide?
  • What to change in your next quote
  • Frequently asked questions
  • Sources and scope

What does quality mean when you buy armored glass?

Imagine that you are going to armor a truck. Two suppliers tell you that their glass is quality. You have to resolve something more specific: what protection that vehicle needs, what options work for it, and how much weight each one would add.

AGP sGlass manufactures armored glass. Its public catalog organizes options by protection level. That gives the buyer a starting point to ask which one works for them and what document supports that option. AGP sGlass public catalog

Take that same question to your next sale. If your client has to explain to their boss why they recommend your offer, can they point out something specific that sets it apart? Give that argument in the quote, where you'll need it. How to get customers to ask for your B2B brand

What proof does each person need to decide?

Think about three people who read the same proposal at different times. Engineering wants to know if the product fits. Purchasing wants to compare two offers under the same conditions. Operations needs to know what happens if the order changes and the delivery date gets closer. The same promise of quality leaves three open questions.

This example is from CRUDA. Roles can change. Choose the interlocutor who can stop the decision and find out what he or she needs to move forward.

What to change in your next quote?

Take a proposal already sent. Ask sales to mark a promise that you usually have to explain over the phone. Then ask someone from operations what exactly they deliver to meet it and what evidence they could share. If you promise reliable deliveries, look for the commitment that you can put in writing and the conditions under which it is held. If you promise the part fits, show what measurement they check before shipping it.

Try it with the person whose turn it is to raise the recommendation. Ask him or her to explain the difference to a colleague with the quote in hand. If you point out specific evidence, give that evidence a fixed place in the document. If you re-read the price, you'll find out what it lacked to warrant another comparison.

Frequently asked questions

Is a certification enough to differentiate my company?

It depends on the decision. If all suppliers must have it to enter the tender, it is valid to participate. It can help distinguish your offer when it covers a specific buyer requirement and it is clear to which version, product or process it applies.

Where should the evidence be shown?

Close to the claim it supports. The quote includes what is necessary to compare. The detailed documentation can be left on an identifiable file or annex so that the buyer can find it when someone asks him to justify the decision.

Sources and scope

  • The AGP sGlass example is based on its public catalog of glass for armored vehicles. The purchasing situation and comparison of offers are hypothetical.

title: Should You Name Your Company After Yourself?
seoTitle: When to Use Your Last Name for Your Business | CRUDA
description: The Mannheim Trading case shows what a founder’s last name can signal. Use a simple buyer test to decide if it belongs in your company name.
html:
Should You Name Your Company After Yourself?

José Mannheim wanted to bring decades of credibility to a new business. He had to decide how much of that history to put up front and what the new business would need to prove for itself.

You are about to present your second company. The first gave you years of work, relationships, and a name that some buyers already know. If you put your last name on the cover, they might immediately understand who is behind it. They may also assume that the company belongs to the previous business or that to resolve any problem they will have to talk to you.

Before choosing what sounds best, imagine that the proposal is forwarded within the buyer's company. What will you understand from who sent you, what can you buy from them, and who will respond if you decide to move forward?

When does it make sense to use your last name for a business?

Use the last name when people who are going to buy already associate it with relevant experience and the new offer can be explained clearly. If the last name suggests that they buy from another company or that they depend on your personal intervention, try a proper name with your career visible in the presentation.

In this article

  • The decision behind Mannheim Trading
  • Three ways to present the same business
  • How to test the name with buyers
  • Frequently asked questions
  • Sources and scope

The decision behind Mannheim Trading

In 1965, José Mannheim and his father founded Autoglass Peruana in Lima. From that company the group known as AGP was born. Decades later, José saw an opportunity in another part of the same industry. Safety glass manufacturers also needed to purchase the materials from which they made their own products. He knew that market and could take advantage of his experience in purchasing and distribution to supply them from a new company. CRUDA Mannheim Trading Case

The question he brought to CRUDA was how to bring that credibility to the new business without building a brand dependent on AGP. The last name made visible the person who knew the industry. "Trading" placed the buyer in front of a different activity. Mannheim Trading could present itself as a materials supplier and explain its offer in its own voice.

The next step was to make that distinction useful. The website shows what the company sells, from glass to the sheets that are placed between layers, and how to request a quote. It also presents services such as technical advice. A manufacturer who recognizes the last name can go from "I know who you are" to "this is what I can ask of you." Mannheim Trading website

The last name resolves part of the presentation. The day a buyer wants to know if a material is useful or when the order arrives, what will matter is the response of the new company. There he begins to form his own reputation.

Three ways to present the same business

Think about a purchasing manager who receives the proposal in the mail. You may know the person, the previous company, or neither. Presenting the same business under three names allows you to see what changes for it.

A first name may work best if you are selling to a buyer who has never heard your last name. And if that buyer does know it, you can still use it at the right moment: the cover letter, the meeting or the company story. The question is how much weight that person needs to carry every time the business presents itself. When to create another brand

How to test the name with buyers

Marty Neumeier proposes evaluating, among other things, whether a name fits with what the company does, if it is distinctive, if it is easy to say and if it allows different ways of expressing itself. For this decision, at CRUDA we would add a commercial test. The Brand Gap, chapter on names

Prepare two versions of the first page of a proposal. In one goes the last name. On the other, a proper name and a line introducing the founder. Use the same offer and the same information in both. Show a version to each buyer and ask them to explain it as if they were to forward it to a colleague.

  • What do you think this company sells?
  • What business do you relate it to?
  • Who would you call if you want a quote or if a problem arises?

If the last name helps locate the trajectory and the buyer understands the offer, there is a reason to use it. If the first thing you ask is whether you are buying from the previous company, you are going to have to clarify the relationship or change how it is presented. And if you think that only you can handle it, the test gives you a business decision. Before printing the name, define who will respond and show that they have the authority to do so. How to introduce the team to your clients

Frequently asked questions

What happens if my last name is known in one market and not in another?

Test the presentation with buyers from both markets. Where it has history, the surname can help explain who is behind it. Where new, the job description and evidence of experience have to do that job.

Does using your last name mean you have to be part of every sale?

The customer forms that expectation based on how the offering is presented and how the company operates. Show who leads the accounts and who can make decisions from the first conversation. If the founder intervenes in specific cases, explain which ones.

Sources and scope

  • Mannheim Trading is a case of CRUDA. Their public site shows the offer and the path to quote. The forwarded proposal scene and the three options in the table are application examples.
  • The naming criteria cited come from The Brand Gap, by Marty Neumeier. The test with buyers is a CRUDA proposal.

title: Marketing is more than managing social media: what makes customers choose your business
seoTitle: What marketing includes beyond social media | CRUDA
description: Product, price, distribution and promotion explained through a burger restaurant. Identify what your business needs before asking for more content.
html:
Marketing is more than managing social media: what makes customers choose your business

Before your first post, you have already made decisions that can help or hurt every sale. A burger restaurant makes this easier to see.

You are opening a burger restaurant.

You have a name. Someone is designing the logo. People are already telling you to start posting videos: meat on the grill, melting cheese, a close-up of the sauce. Someone knows how to get views.

But some questions remain unanswered.

Who lives or works nearby? Where do they eat lunch? What can they spend? Do they want a table or a quick takeaway? Are there families, offices, students? What options do they have, and what is missing?

The answers could change your menu, prices, opening hours and even your decision to lease that space.

That is marketing, too. It starts before you have an Instagram account.

If you run an industrial business, an architecture practice or a service company, the problem is similar. You can spend heavily promoting an offer without understanding the person who should buy it.

Marketing includes understanding customers, developing an offer, setting its price, making it available to buy and communicating its value. Social media can contribute to that work. It does not represent all of it.

In this article

  • What marketing means in practice
  • Research before the product
  • The four Ps, without the jargon
  • What you buy when you buy marketing
  • Brand, name, logo and experience
  • When people need what you sell, do they remember you?
  • What Liquid Death teaches us
  • What needs to change in your business
  • Frequently asked questions

What does marketing mean in practice?

At CRUDA, we explain it this way: understand whom you want to sell to, then make decisions that give them a valuable offer they can buy and want to return to.

That involves more than promoting whatever you have already decided to produce. Sometimes it means changing it.

Philip Kotler is one of the authors who helped teach marketing to generations of professionals. In his textbook with Gary Armstrong, the starting point is creating value for customers and building relationships that also generate value for the business. In everyday language: offer something another person finds useful and build a business around that exchange. Source: chapter published by Pearson.

The American Marketing Association, a professional association for the discipline, also includes creating and delivering offers alongside communicating them. Its definition does not limit marketing to advertising. Source: AMA definition.

Back to the restaurant. You might make an excellent burger and open in an area where most people have twenty minutes for lunch. If your service takes forty, no video of melting cheese will fix that problem.

The recipe might be right. The offer, for that situation, might be wrong.

Before defining the product, understand who will buy it

Researching local customers is part of developing the product. It also informs price, location, service and communication.

For this hypothetical restaurant, we would start by walking the neighborhood at different times, observing alternatives and talking to potential customers.

Asking “Would you like a burger restaurant here?” tells you little. Someone can love the idea and never buy.

Understand an actual choice instead:

  • Where did you eat lunch yesterday, and why did you choose it?
  • How much time did you have, and what did you end up paying?
  • What other option did you consider?
  • What usually goes wrong when you order food?

You might discover there is no shortage of burgers. What is missing is lunch that arrives on time, is easy to order and has a clear total price from the start.

That finding could change the menu, meal deals and ordering system. You have not written an ad yet, but you are already doing marketing.

Research is useful when it can change a decision. If all you want is confirmation of your idea, you are looking for approval.

The same applies to an established business. Customers buying one product line does not guarantee they want the next. Before launching, understand what it would solve and what alternative it would compete against.

The four Ps: what you sell, what it costs, how people buy and how they hear about it

Product, price, place and promotion organize the marketing mix: decisions about the offer you bring to market. They are not the entire definition of marketing. They are a useful way to organize part of the work.

“Place” means distribution: where and how the offer reaches the buyer.

DecisionThe owner's questionAt the burger restaurant
ProductWhat does the customer need, and what will we offer?A lunch that is easy to choose, receive and eat.
PriceWhat do people pay, and what do they believe they get?A meal deal with a clear total price and terms.
PlaceWhere, when and how can people buy?The restaurant, digital orders, hours and delivery area.
PromotionHow do people discover and consider us?Communication that makes the offer visible and desirable.

Product: the burger has to fit the customer's life

Can someone eat it without making a mess before a meeting? Is there an option for the vegetarian in the group? Does it travel well on a twenty-minute delivery ride?

A burger designed to be eaten at a table may not travel well. A huge menu can make choosing harder and slow down the kitchen.

Customer research does not come afterward, simply to work out how to persuade people. It helps decide what to offer.

Your taste can start the business. It cannot replace knowing the customer.

In services, the equivalent is defining scope, timing and responsibilities around what the buyer needs to solve. “We do everything” does not necessarily make buying easier.

Price: customers compare what they pay with what they believe they receive

The restaurant advertises an attractive price. Add a drink, fries and delivery, and the total looks very different.

The final price may be reasonable. Discovering it that way can still undermine trust.

The opposite happens too: an offer seems expensive until you understand what is included.

Pricing involves costs and margins, but also alternatives and perceived value: what customers think the offer is worth. Copying a competitor or charging more because “we are premium” is not a substitute for that work.

In B2B—when one business sells to another—the question is just as concrete: does the buyer understand the difference between your proposal and the cheaper one?

If a meaningful difference exists but is not understood, communication may be missing. If there is no relevant difference for that buyer, new wording will not create one.

Place: make buying possible and easy

Someone watches the video and wants to order. They visit the profile, cannot find the menu, send a message and get an answer an hour later. Then they discover delivery is unavailable in their area.

Communication created interest. The business could not serve it.

Location, delivery coverage, hours and availability determine how the offer reaches the market. In another industry, the obstacle may be a distributor without stock or a quote that takes a week.

Marketing needs to identify those difficulties and work with the people who can solve them. Operations, sales and technology do not therefore have to report to marketing. The buyer's experience crosses the whole company.

Promotion: give someone a reason to pay attention

Now we reach advertising, content, public relations, influencer marketing, referral programs and SEO—the work of helping people find you in search engines—among other tools. They can all contribute to promotion. They are not the whole of marketing.

Our restaurant has something specific to communicate: an easy-to-order lunch for people working nearby. A video can make it desirable. An ad can reach more people. A recommendation can give someone confidence to try it.

This is important work. The mistake is expecting it to compensate indefinitely for an unresolved offer.

Mark Ritson, a marketing educator and consultant, criticizes proposals that replace the four Ps with digital activities and leave out price, product and distribution. In our example, a plan for posting and generating inquiries is still incomplete if nobody asks what we sell, what it costs or how people buy it. Source: Ritson's own article.

What are you buying when you buy “marketing”?

It depends. That ambiguity costs money.

One person may be excellent at producing videos. Another can manage ads. Another can design a visual identity. These are different capabilities.

A hook, for example, is an opening designed to keep someone watching or reading. It might be a good question, an unexpected scene or a relevant statement. Knowing how to create one is useful. It does not, by itself, demonstrate the ability to research buyers, review prices or develop an offer.

If you hire someone to create content, you need good content. Do not assume you have also bought a complete business strategy.

Before comparing proposals, ask which decisions each provider will address. Otherwise, you can end up comparing numbers of posts when you needed to compare capabilities.

Where do the brand, name and logo fit?

The restaurant must decide what it wants to be remembered for. Solving weekday lunch? Being the place to meet friends? Offering a special dining experience?

At CRUDA, positioning means the space you want to occupy in your customer's mind and, where appropriate, their heart.

Choosing that space has consequences. If you want to be the reliable lunch option, punctuality matters. If you want friends to stay for a while, space and service matter.

A brand develops through what people recognize, expect and associate with the business. Identity is the set of elements used to present it and make it recognizable. They are not exactly the same thing.

WorkWhat it helps the business do
Brand strategyDecide what we want to mean to customers and how to sustain it.
Brand architectureDecide whether another offer uses the same name, an extension or a separate brand.
NamingChoose the name that identifies the offer.
Visual and verbal identityBuild a recognizable appearance and way of speaking.
CopywritingWrite to explain, create interest and help people make a decision.
Digital experienceMake viewing the menu, choosing and ordering straightforward.
Design systemKeep rules and components consistent across screens, buttons and forms.
Communication strategyDecide what to explain, to whom, where and why.
Public relations, or PRDevelop relationships and opportunities for presence in media and other relevant settings.
Content and advertisingCreate and distribute messages that support those goals.

These are not identical building blocks: some are strategies, others disciplines or systems. They work together.

A website can communicate and sell. A menu can express a personality and make choosing easier. Form has practical consequences.

Substance before appearance: understand what you want to express before deciding how it looks.

If you are considering an identity change, first distinguish whether you need a rebrand or a clearer explanation of what your company already does.

When someone needs what you sell, do they remember your business?

Not everyone who sees a post wants a burger at that moment.

Some have just eaten. Others discover you on Tuesday but are going out with friends on Friday.

If you evaluate every contact solely by immediate purchases, you miss part of the job: making the brand come to mind when a need arises.

“Where can we order something that will arrive before the meeting?”

Does your name come up?

“One of our friends is vegetarian. Where can we all eat?”

Is your restaurant associated with that possibility?

That is what building associations in memory means: connecting a brand with a situation someone may encounter. Recognizing the logo when it is in front of them is not enough. Remembering it when they are not looking at your advertising matters too.

Jon Lombardo and Peter Weinberg, cofounders of research company Evidenza, explain this connection between memory and buying. Their work helps frame a practical question: which situations should make someone think of your business? This section's opening question is CRUDA's editorial interpretation, not a direct quotation. Source: Lombardo and Weinberg.

If you sell machinery or services purchased only every few years, many future customers will not be shopping today. You can become known and understood before they begin looking for suppliers.

This distinction is the starting point for exploring the so-called 95–5 rule in another article. Here, the principle matters: being outside a buying window does not mean someone is not a future customer. We will not treat those percentages as universal or as the percentage who actually purchase.

Attention is not the same as brand equity

The restaurant posts a funny video. Thousands see it. What happened to the brand?

It may have become associated with something desirable. It may have gone unnoticed behind the joke. It may have put people off.

Views alone cannot distinguish those outcomes.

Brand equity refers to the additional value associated with being that brand: how its name and associations change people's response. It is not another word for fame or an isolated positive reaction.

Brand sentiment addresses a different question: how people feel about it. That can include liking, indifference, rejection or nostalgia. Understanding it takes research; visible comments do not automatically represent all buyers.

More people knowing you does not guarantee more people wanting to choose you. That is why “there is no such thing as bad publicity” is not a serious principle for running a company.

Attention creates an opportunity. What people understand and remember afterward matters. We will explore that distinction separately while keeping this article focused on the full responsibility of marketing.

Liquid Death: asking an agency to make something interesting after everything is decided

Liquid Death is an American brand that began selling canned water. Its name and presentation depart from the calm, healthy image usually associated with water.

Founder Mike Cessario came from advertising: his work involved finding ways to make other companies' products interesting.

In his conversation with Jon Evans, host of the marketing podcast Uncensored CMO, he describes a sequence that deserves attention. A company decides on the product and name, commissions the design and then seeks an agency to make people care. His alternative is to involve people who understand culture and behavior earlier, while they can still influence the offer and its presentation. This paraphrases the argument recorded in our listening notes; it is not a verbatim quotation. Original interview.

The problem is not having a business degree or hiring a designer. It is closing important decisions without sufficiently considering the buyer, then asking communication to bridge that gap.

At our restaurant, that would mean choosing the location, menu, price and service around the owner's preferences. When sales prove difficult, the agency is asked to “make something go viral.”

Bring the right people in earlier and you can still change the meal deal, simplify ordering or discover an underserved occasion. Creativity can help shape the offer as well as produce the ad.

An agency can help explain an offer and make it desirable. Do not expect it to invent relevance while being unable to change anything you offer.

We explore the case in Liquid Death: marketing starts before launch.

Does that mean content does not matter?

It matters. A valuable offer can go unnoticed or be poorly explained.

Gary Vaynerchuk, known as GaryVee, is an entrepreneur and communicator who consistently advocates producing content. He has also stated that great marketing will not fix a bad product. Even a prominent advocate for content recognizes communication cannot solve everything. Original post.

Our precise formulation is this: posting more does not, by itself, fix an unwanted offer, a misunderstood price or a difficult purchase. Researching and changing those decisions is marketing too.

You do not have to wait until everything is perfect. The questions you receive can improve the offer and how you explain it.

Rory Sutherland, an Ogilvy advertising executive who explores how perception influences decisions, adds another nuance: communication can change the value we attribute to something without physically changing the product. At our restaurant, explaining a relevant difference can help people appreciate it. That matters; it does not remove the obligation to deliver what was promised. Sutherland's TED talk.

Before asking for more content, identify the difficulty

“We need more sales” is a goal. It does not yet explain what is preventing it.

What you observeWhat to investigate
People do not know us.How potential buyers discover their options.
They know us but do not consider us.When we come to mind and what people expect from us.
They inquire but do not understand the offer.What is confusing or missing.
They compare only on price.Which differences they value and can verify.
They want to proceed but abandon the purchase.Which condition, doubt or step gets in the way.
They buy once and do not return.What they experienced and what they expected.

These are research questions, not automatic diagnoses.

At your next meeting, reconstruct a purchase that happened and one that fell through. What each person needed. How they arrived. What they compared. What they asked. What influenced the decision.

Separate what you know from what you assume. Then choose what to change, who should participate and what signal would show improvement.

You might need more visibility. You might need a simpler offer, revised terms or an easier purchase.

If the problem is that everyone promises the same thing, continue with differentiating a B2B company beyond “quality and service”.

Frequently asked questions

Is marketing the same as advertising?

No. Advertising helps communicate an offer. Marketing also includes understanding the buyer and working on the offer, price and distribution.

Is customer research part of product development?

Yes. Understanding needs, habits and alternatives helps determine what to offer. That research can also change pricing, sales channels and communication.

Can social media generate sales?

It can contribute to sales and, depending on the business, act as a sales channel. Results also depend on the offer, availability and ease of purchase.

Do I need a logo before doing marketing?

No. Researching buyers, choosing an offer and defining how to sell it are already marketing decisions. Identity helps express that offer and make it recognizable.

Should all marketing generate immediate sales?

Different activities serve different purposes. Some help convert current interest; others build knowledge and associations for future decisions. Evaluate them against their objective and connection to the business.

Does a small business need all of this?

It already makes these decisions, even without using these names. It has an offer, a price and a way to sell and communicate. Reviewing them together helps identify priorities without hiring every specialty at once.

The restaurant may need a great video.

It may also need a clearer menu, a meal deal suited to the neighborhood, an easier way to order or a reason to be remembered next Friday.

Marketing means being able to tell the difference.

title: What should you research before launching a new business line?
seoTitle: Research before launching a new business line | CRUDA
description: Use CRUDA’s five Cs to research buyers, alternatives, pricing, and delivery before launching a business line. A practical example and a first test.
html:
What should you research before launching a new business line?

Your company already has customers. Before asking them to buy something new, understand how they solve that problem today.

The conversation might begin in a leadership meeting. We have the suppliers, we understand the product, and we already sell to these companies. If we add this line, they should buy it from us too.

There may be an opportunity. There is also an assumption worth examining before commissioning a name, expanding the catalog, or committing to inventory. Trust earned in one purchase does not yet explain how someone makes another.

Before launching a new business line, research who faces the problem, how they solve it today, what triggers a purchase, who approves it, and what would make them change suppliers. Compare those answers with your delivery capacity and the economics of the business. The research should inform decisions about the offer, price, sales channel, and the first test you need to run.

At CRUDA, we organize that conversation through five perspectives. We call them Culture, Context, Category, Company, and Customer. Below, we apply them to a business that already sells and wants to grow.

In this article

  • When knowing the product seems sufficient
  • What to examine through the five Cs
  • How to ask questions that go beyond compliments
  • What to test before increasing the investment
  • The decision that should change
  • Frequently asked questions and sources

When knowing the product seems sufficient

Imagine a company that sells equipment for commercial kitchens. Its customers are restaurants and hotels. Leadership wants to add preventive maintenance for a monthly fee. The company understands the equipment, carries spare parts, and already handles technical questions.

This is a hypothetical example. It lets us follow one decision from beginning to end.

Internally, the proposal looks reasonable. The customer pays every month and avoids problems. The company adds recurring revenue and uses capabilities it already has.

Now listen to three people inside a hotel. The head chef needs the oven working throughout dinner service. The maintenance manager has a trusted technician who knows the installation. Finance wants to understand what the fee covers and which repairs cost extra.

Selling the oven and selling maintenance involves answering different questions. The person who recommended buying the equipment may have little involvement in procuring the service. Existing trust can help you get a conversation. To move forward, the new offer has to make sense in this particular purchase.

Research begins there. What would the company need to understand to design a service someone could purchase, use, and justify to their manager?

What to examine through the five Cs

Useful research takes a decision leadership is about to make and examines it from several perspectives. This is our practical use of the five Cs. The questions and application express CRUDA's editorial judgment.

Culture — What feels normal in this market

How do people usually get things done? Perhaps the manager always calls the same technician because they trust him and can reach him on a Saturday. Perhaps accepting a monthly fee means justifying an expense that previously required approval only when something broke.

To understand that habit, ask how they chose their current provider and what they value about the relationship. The familiar technician is part of your actual competition, even if your company has a stronger presentation and more employees.

Context — When the need appears

A hotel that is opening, one renovating its kitchen, and one that has just suffered a breakdown may evaluate the same service differently. Find out what was happening when the last decision was made.

This may change when you sell. Perhaps maintenance should be introduced during installation, while the operation is being organized. Or after an inspection, when there is a visible problem the customer can assess. Those are hypotheses to investigate.

Category — Which alternatives buyers compare

The alternative might be a contract with another provider, a technician hired per visit, the internal team, or continuing to repair things when they break. Ask the buyer to explain which options they considered and why they rejected each one.

The SBA, the US agency supporting small businesses, includes demand, available alternatives, and pricing among its research questions. It also distinguishes existing data from direct research with buyers. That distinction helps connect market context with actual decisions. SBA guide

Company — What your business can sustain

Who answers outside normal hours? How many customers can one technician cover? How far can they travel? Are spare parts available? What does a faster response promise cost?

These questions have to be answered inside the operation. If the commercial appeal depends on weekend support, someone needs to cost and organize it. It is part of the product you are designing.

We develop the same thinking in our article on marketing, product, price, and distribution. Research can change what you sell before it changes how you advertise it.

Customer — Who experiences the problem and who pays

At the hotel, the kitchen may experience the problem, maintenance may evaluate the solution, and finance may approve the commitment. Research all three perspectives when they have a real role.

Who asked to look for alternatives? What did each person need to see? Who could stop the purchase? Who receives the complaint if the service fails? Those answers help you build an offer that can travel through the customer's organization.

From five perspectives to a decision

PerspectiveWhat you want to learnWhat could change
CultureWhy they trust their usual technicianContinuity of contact and how you introduce your team
ContextWhen they review maintenance arrangementsWhen you offer the service
CategoryWhat they compare with a monthly feeThe pricing structure and how you explain it
CompanyWhat support you can deliver profitablyCoverage, hours, and conditions
CustomerWho recommends, uses, and approvesThe evidence each person needs

This matrix is a CRUDA tool applied to the hypothetical example. Each finding should be traceable to a conversation, a record, or an operational check. An entry filled with intuition remains a hypothesis.

How to ask questions that go beyond compliments

“Would you like us to offer maintenance?” leaves plenty of room for a polite response. Saying yes is easy when there is no contract, internal decision, or budget at stake yet.

Try reconstructing the most recent purchase or breakdown. What happened? Who did they call first? How long did they wait? What information did they seek? Who approved the expense? What made them stay with that provider?

Then you can show a concrete proposal. What it includes, what it costs, when the team responds, and what is excluded. Ask what they would need to review to purchase it and who else should see it. Record what prevents them from moving forward too.

Start with existing customers, lost opportunities, and companies choosing another solution today. Record the type of buyer in each conversation. Several interviews with one profile may reveal a tension you later need to measure with an appropriate sample. An enthusiastic conversation cannot establish market size.

Public conversations can help you find vocabulary, complaints, and questions. Industry data helps establish context. To decide whether your service fits, you need to get closer to the actual buying situation. Each source has value for the questions it can answer.

What to test before increasing the investment

Return to the hotel. Suppose the conversations reveal concern about weekend breakdowns. Your team confirms it can cover a limited area with certain parts available.

You can design a limited test in that area. Before offering it, agree on scope, price, exclusions, capacity, and an accountable service lead. Define the outcome that would justify expansion and the signal that would require a correction.

The test might show interest converting into contracts under those conditions. It might also reveal that everyone wants availability, but few will accept the price needed to sustain it. Or that customers value a scheduled inspection more than a promise of emergency support.

Each result calls for different work. Adjusting coverage, changing the offer, reviewing costs, or dropping a promise the company cannot yet deliver. It helps to make that decision while the investment is manageable.

The pilot provides evidence for that segment under those conditions. Before projecting into other markets or customers, examine what changes in distances, costs, habits, and procurement.

The decision that should change

Before starting, write one sentence with your team. “We are deciding whether to offer monthly maintenance to hotels in this area, under these conditions.” At the end, explain what you retained, what you changed, and what evidence supports it.

In our example, leadership might move from “sell maintenance to all our customers” to “test a scheduled service with nearby hotels, offered during installation with defined coverage.” That precision makes it possible to budget, organize delivery, and communicate something understandable.

Another question follows. Does the new line need its own name? That decision should consider the trust that already exists and what the buyer needs to recognize. We explore it in brand architecture.

CRUDA's approach begins with the purchase you want to understand. Curiosity serves the business when it helps challenge an internal certainty and design an offer the company can sustain.

Frequently asked questions

What should I research first if I already have customers?

How they currently solve the problem your new line would address. Find out who participates, what triggers the purchase, which alternatives they compare, and what conditions they need to change.

How many interviews do I need?

That depends on the diversity of buyers and the risk of the decision. An initial qualitative round can reveal differences and questions. Estimating demand or proportions requires an appropriate design and sample. Always explain the limits of what you learned.

Can research change the price or the service too?

Yes. It may reveal that the customer values different coverage, needs another way to pay, or requires a capability you still need to develop. That is a reason to research before finalizing the offer and campaign.

Can I research using social comments and AI tools?

They can help uncover questions and organize material. Verify sources and context, then test the hypotheses against real buyers and your company's records. Public comments carry participation biases and do not automatically represent your market.

Sources and scope

The applied five Cs method and decision recommendations express CRUDA's judgment. The kitchen equipment company and hotel are hypothetical examples, with no commercial results attributed to clients. The SBA guide provides methodological context on demand, alternatives, and direct research. Its US data does not estimate a Latin American market. Primary source
